title: A Letter to God
short: Lencho's unshakable faith and the irony that follows it.
lede: G. L. Fuentes. A farmer, a hailstorm, a letter — and one of the sharpest ironies in the syllabus.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts and one 5-mark value-based long answer. The **irony** is always the question.
Know the numbers cold: Lencho asked for **one hundred pesos**, received **seventy**, and accused the post office employees of being *'a bunch of crooks'*.
concepts: **1. Summary.** Lencho, a simple hardworking farmer, lives on the crest of a low hill in a Latin American valley, with his cornfield ripening and dotted with flowers. Rain comes — but it turns into a **hailstorm** that destroys the crop completely. Lencho's only hope is God, so he writes a letter asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again and to live until the next harvest. The postmaster, a fat, amiable fellow, is moved by the farmer's faith, collects **seventy pesos** from his employees and friends, and sends the money in a letter signed *'God'*. Lencho, on receiving the letter, is not surprised, but is angry at the shortfall: he writes a second letter asking God to send the rest directly, because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.

**2. Characters.** **Lencho** — a simple, hardworking, unquestioning man of faith; his faith is absolute but so is his innocence. **The postmaster** — kind, generous and witty; he does not want to shake the farmer's faith in God. **The employees and friends of the post office** — they contribute out of charity, and are unjustly called crooks.

**3. Themes.** **Unshakable faith** — Lencho never doubts that God will answer. **Irony** — the very people who helped him are the ones he calls crooks. **Human kindness and generosity** — the postmaster's act is not duty but compassion. **The gap between faith and reality.**
tricks: - The word **'crooks'** in the last line is the exam favourite. It means dishonest people — and the irony is that Lencho says it about the men who gave him money.
- **Two ironies, not one:** the hailstorm destroys the crop that the rain was supposed to save; and the helpers are accused of theft.
- Lencho is *not* grateful in the second letter — that surprise is worth a mark.
mistakes: - Saying Lencho received one hundred pesos. He received **seventy**.
- Describing the postmaster as Lencho's relative or a government official on duty. He acted **out of personal kindness**.
- Missing the word **'amiable'** when describing the postmaster — examiners look for textual detail.

qa.q: Why did Lencho say the post office employees were a bunch of crooks?
qa.a: Because he had asked God for one hundred pesos and received only seventy. His faith was so absolute that he could not believe God had made a mistake or had sent less, so he concluded that the post office employees must have taken the remaining thirty pesos. The irony is that these were the very men who had collected the money for him out of charity.

qa.q: What made the postmaster decide to help Lencho?
qa.a: He was moved by the farmer's unshakable faith in God. He did not want to shake that faith, so he collected money from his employees and friends, gave part of his own salary, and sent it to Lencho in a letter signed 'God'.

qa.q: 'The story is built around two ironies.' Explain with reference to the text.
a: The first irony is in the weather: Lencho's field needed rain, and rain did come — but it turned into a hailstorm that destroyed the entire crop. The very thing that promised a good harvest took it away.

The second irony is in the ending: the post office employees, moved by Lencho's faith, collected seventy pesos and sent them to him. Lencho, finding the amount short, wrote back accusing those same men of stealing the money and calling them 'a bunch of crooks'. The helpers become the accused thieves, and the man who never doubted God doubts the honesty of human beings.

qa.q: Was Lencho surprised to find a letter with money in it? What made him angry?
qa.a: No, he was not surprised at all — he had expected an answer from God, and his confidence in God was so complete that receiving a reply seemed natural. What made him angry was that the envelope contained only seventy pesos instead of the hundred he had asked for. He was certain that God could not have made a mistake, so he concluded that the post office employees had taken the rest.

title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
short: Apartheid, the inauguration of 1994 and what freedom came to mean.
lede: An extract from Mandela's autobiography *Long Walk to Freedom*. Dates and definitions carry the marks.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts and one 5-mark long answer on the meaning of freedom or on courage.
**10 May 1994** — the inauguration at the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria — is the anchor date.
Know the three national anthems, the meaning of **apartheid**, and the two obligations.
concepts: **1. Summary.** On **10 May 1994**, Nelson Mandela was sworn in as South Africa's first black President at the **Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria**, before an international gathering of leaders. The day marked the end of **apartheid** — a political system that separated people according to race — and the birth of a new, democratic, non-racial nation. **Three national anthems** were sung: *'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika'* and *'Morena'* by the blacks, *'Die Stem'* the old anthem of the Republic, and the new combined anthem. Mandela reflects on the day: a beautiful autumn day, but for the whites a symbol of victory and for the blacks a symbol of a new beginning. He recalls his own journey from a frightened young man to a bold one, and thanks the **international presence**, which he sees as a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity.

**2. Courage and oppression.** Mandela says that he learned that **courage was not the absence of fear but the triumph over it** — the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear. Decades of oppression made him hunger for freedom, not just for himself but for all his people. He says that **the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity**: the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness, and is not truly free; the oppressed, robbed of his dignity, is also not free.

**3. The twin obligations.** Every man has **two obligations**: the first to his **family** — his parents, his wife and children; the second to his **people**, his community and his country. In a civil and humane society each man is able to fulfil both. In South Africa under apartheid, a man like Mandela who tried to live as a human being was **punished and isolated**, and could not fulfil either obligation.

**4. The meaning of freedom.** As a boy, freedom meant running in the fields, swimming in the stream and roasting mealies under the stars. As a student, it meant staying out at night, reading what he pleased and going where he liked — **transitory freedoms**. As a young man he yearned for the honourable freedoms of achieving his potential, of earning his keep, of marrying and having a family. Only later did he understand that **freedom is indivisible** — the chains on any one of his people were chains on all of them. He says that freedom was not just to throw off one's chains, but **to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others**. His long walk is not yet ended.
tricks: - **Courage = triumph over fear, not absence of fear.** That sentence is asked repeatedly and must be quoted nearly word-for-word.
- **Two obligations: family and people.** In apartheid South Africa, a man could not discharge both.
- **Freedom changed meaning with age:** boyhood = physical freedom, youth = honourable freedoms, later = freedom of the whole people.
mistakes: - Giving the inauguration date as 10 May 1995. It is **1994**.
- Saying South Africa has two national anthems. **Three** were sung that day.
- Defining apartheid as segregation only. The textbook calls it a **political system that separates people according to race**.

qa.q: What does courage mean to Mandela?
qa.a: For Mandela, courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it. The brave man is not the one who does not feel afraid, but the one who conquers that fear. He says he felt fear more times than he can remember, and it was this repeated conquest of fear that made him bold.

qa.q: What 'twin obligations' does Mandela mention?
qa.a: The first obligation is to his family — his parents, his wife and children. The second is to his people, his community and his country. In a civil and humane society each person can fulfil both, but in South Africa under apartheid, a man like Mandela who tried to live as a human being was punished and isolated, and could not discharge either obligation.

qa.q: How did Mandela's understanding of freedom change with age and experience?
a: **As a boy** in the villages of Umtata, freedom meant being able to run in the fields near his mother's hut, to swim in the stream, to roast mealies under the stars and to ride the broad backs of slow-moving bulls. It was the freedom of a child, and it seemed boundless.
**As a student** he wanted the transitory freedoms of staying out at night, reading what he pleased and going where he liked.
**As a young man** he yearned for the honourable freedoms — of achieving his potential, of earning his keep, of marrying and having a family, of living lawfully in a law-abiding society.

**Later** he realised that these were only illusory, because he was not free and neither were his people. He came to understand that **freedom is indivisible**: the chains on any one of his people were chains on all of them. He saw that the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity, and that freedom is not merely to throw off one's chains but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.

qa.q: Why did such a large number of international leaders attend the inauguration? What did it signify?
qa.a: It signified the recognition by the international community of the birth of a free, democratic, non-racial South Africa, and a common victory for justice, for peace and for human dignity. The presence of leaders of many nations showed that the end of apartheid was not only a South African event but a triumph of values shared by the whole world.

qa.q: Why does Mandela say that the oppressor is also not free?
qa.a: Because the oppressor is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness. A man who takes away another man's freedom is himself deprived of his own humanity, so the oppressor and the oppressed are both robbed of what makes them human.

title: Two Stories about Flying
short: His First Flight by O'Flaherty and The Black Aeroplane by Forsyth.
lede: Two stories, one theme: fear overcome. The seagull is the more frequently examined of the two.
lens: Extracts come from either story; know both well enough to identify which one is quoted.
**His First Flight** — Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull afraid to fly. **The Black Aeroplane** — Frederick Forsyth, a pilot in a storm helped by a mysterious black aeroplane.
concepts: **1. His First Flight — summary.** A young seagull is alone on his ledge, afraid to fly, while his two brothers and sister have already flown away the day before. His parents have scolded him and threatened to let him starve on the ledge unless he flies. His siblings taunt him by calling him 'Ga-ga'. After **twenty-four hours** of hunger and fear, his mother tears a piece of fish and stands on the ledge, and the sight of the food maddens him. He dives at her, his hunger overcomes his fear, and he falls outward into space. The air rushes against his feathers, he flaps his wings and finds himself soaring. His family screams around him, praising him and offering scraps of fish. He then flies with them, sinks tired onto the water, and though afraid at first, learns to float — his **first flight is complete**.

**2. The Black Aeroplane — summary.** The narrator, flying an old Dakota aeroplane from France to England to spend a breakfast of bacon and eggs with his family, flies into a storm. The clouds are black, his compass and radio fail, and he has only enough fuel for five or ten minutes. He sees a **black aeroplane** with no lights on its wings, and the pilot waves for him to follow. He follows it through the storm until he runs out of fuel, and then the black plane disappears. He lands safely and asks the woman in the control centre where the other pilot is. She says the sky was empty — **there was no other aeroplane** that night, and no other plane on the radar. The narrator looks up and wonders who helped him.

**3. Common theme.** Both stories are about **facing fear and finding the strength to overcome it**. The seagull is helped by hunger and by his mother's example; the pilot is helped — or so he believes — by another pilot. Both suggest that the help we need is sometimes already within us.
tricks: - **Twenty-four hours** on the ledge is the key number in *His First Flight*.
- The seagull's fear breaks when he sees the **fish**, not when his parents scold him.
- In *The Black Aeroplane*, the control-centre woman says there was **no other plane** — that ambiguity is the point of the ending.
mistakes: - Confusing the two authors: **O'Flaherty** wrote *His First Flight*, **Forsyth** wrote *The Black Aeroplane*.
- Saying the seagull flew because his father threatened him. It was **hunger and the sight of food**.
- Naming the Dakota a fighter plane. It is an **old Dakota** carrying the narrator home.

qa.q: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly? What compelled him to finally make the flight?
qa.a: He was afraid because he felt certain that his wings would never support him, and because his siblings had already flown while he was left behind on the ledge. What compelled him to fly was hunger: when his mother tore a piece of fish and stood on the ledge, the sight of the food maddened him, and he dived at it. In that dive he fell outward into space and, flapping his wings, found that he could fly.

qa.q: Describe the help the pilot received during the storm in 'The Black Aeroplane'.
qa.a: When his instruments failed and he ran low on fuel, he saw a black aeroplane with no lights on its wings. Its pilot waved to him and led him through the storm until the narrator came out of the clouds and could see the runway. When he landed and asked the woman in the control centre about the other pilot, she told him there had been no other aeroplane in the sky that night, and no other plane on her radar.

qa.q: 'Both the stories are about overcoming fear.' Justify with reference to the two stories.
a: In **His First Flight**, the young seagull is paralysed by fear while his brothers and sister fly. His parents scold him and his siblings taunt him, but fear keeps him on the ledge for twenty-four hours. Only extreme hunger, and the sight of his mother with a piece of fish, drive him to dive — and in that desperate moment he discovers that his wings do support him. His fear is overcome by necessity and by the example of his family.

In **The Black Aeroplane**, the narrator is an experienced pilot, but the storm terrifies him: the compass and radio fail, he cannot see anything, and he has only a few minutes of fuel left. His fear is overcome by following the mysterious black aeroplane, whose pilot leads him out of the storm and vanishes. He never finds out who helped him, which suggests that the courage came from within.
In both stories, fear is conquered only by taking the leap — the seagull by diving, the pilot by following into the dark — and in both the reward is a safe arrival.

qa.q: How did the seagull's family react when he flew for the first time?
qa.a: They screamed around him, praising him and offering him scraps of fish. They landed ahead of him on the water, beckoning him to join them, and when he finally sank tired onto the sea and floated, they praised him again — his first flight was complete.

title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
short: A thirteen-year-old's first diary entries and her punishment essay.
lede: Anne Frank's own words. Two essays and one teacher are the whole plot — but the voice is what is examined.
lens: Reference-to-context extracts, usually from the opening passage about why she keeps a diary, or from the essay 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'.
Know why she began the diary, why she needed a friend, and what Mr Keesing asked her to write about.
concepts: **1. Summary.** Thirteen-year-old Anne Frank begins her diary, which she names **Kitty**, on her thirteenth birthday. She explains that **'paper has more patience than people'**: she has a loving family, an adoring father and mother, a sixteen-year-old sister Margot, about thirty friends and many admirers, but no **true friend** to whom she can confide her innermost thoughts. Her grandmother, whom she loved very much, died in January 1942; Anne's entry of June 1942 is followed by her family going into hiding in July. She is a student in a Jewish secondary school in Amsterdam.

**2. The essays.** Her mathematics teacher, **Mr Keesing**, is annoyed by her talking in class and assigns her an essay titled **'A Chatterbox'**. Anne writes three pages and argues that talking is a student's trait and that she would try to keep it under control, but that she would never be able to cure herself of the habit since her mother talks as much as she does — and there is little one can do about inherited traits. Mr Keesing takes the joke in the right spirit. The next time she talks he assigns **'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'**. The third time he sets **'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'** as punishment, this time to be written in verse. Anne's friend **Sanne** helps, and Anne writes the poem about a mother duck and a father swan whose three ducklings are bitten to death because they quacked too much. Mr Keesing reads it to his own class and to another class, adds his own comments, and from then on allows Anne to talk in class and never gives her any extra homework. To Anne he is **'the nicest teacher'** she has ever met.

**3. Themes.** The **need for a friend and for a private voice**; **the gap between the self one shows and the self one feels**; **humour as a defence**; and the shadow of the **Jewish experience under Nazi rule**, which the diary entries only hint at.
tricks: - **'Paper has more patience than people'** — the single most quoted line from this chapter; learn it exactly.
- **Three essays in order:** A Chatterbox → An Incorrigible Chatterbox → Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox.
- Anne argues her talking is an **inherited trait** from her mother — that argument is what wins Mr Keesing over.
mistakes: - Saying Anne had no friends at all. She had about thirty friends and admirers, but **no true friend** to confide in.
- Naming the diary 'Anne'. She named it **Kitty**.
- Describing Mr Keesing as strict and unkind throughout. He turns out to be, in Anne's words, **the nicest teacher**.

qa.q: What argument did Anne make in her first essay, 'A Chatterbox'?
qa.a: She argued that talking is a student's trait and that she would try to keep it under control, but that she would never be able to cure herself completely of the habit, because her mother talks as much as she does. She added that there is little one can do about inherited traits — an argument which Mr Keesing took in the right spirit.

qa.q: Describe Mr Keesing and how his attitude towards Anne changed.
a: **Mr Keesing** was Anne's mathematics teacher, an old-fashioned teacher who was annoyed by her constant talking in class. He punished her by assigning an essay titled 'A Chatterbox'.

**Anne's response:** she wrote three pages, admitting the habit but arguing that talking is a student's trait and that her mother talks as much as she does, so it is an inherited trait and there is little one can do about it. Mr Keesing took the joke in the right spirit.

**The second and third essays:** when she talked again he assigned 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox', and the third time he set 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox' — this time in verse. With the help of her friend Sanne, Anne wrote a comic poem about a mother duck and a father swan whose three ducklings are bitten to death by the swan for quacking too much.

**The change:** Mr Keesing read the poem to his own class and then to another class, adding his own comments, and laughed at it. From then on he allowed Anne to talk in class and never gave her extra homework again. Anne calls him the nicest teacher she ever met.

title: Glimpses of India
short: Goa's bakers, Assam's tea country and Coorg's people.
lede: Three short travel pieces in one chapter. Each is examined separately, so treat them as three mini-chapters.
lens: Extracts and short answers are set from any one of the three parts; the question usually names the part.
**A Baker from Goa** — Lucio Rodrigues. **Coorg** — Lokesh Abrol. **Tea from Assam** — Arup Kumar Datta.
concepts: **1. A Baker from Goa (Lucio Rodrigues).** In the old days of Portuguese rule, bakers — known as **pader** — were an important part of Goan life. Their arrival was announced by the **'jang, jhang, jhang'** of the bamboo staff they carried, one hand on the basket of loaves and the other banging the staff on the ground. Children ran to meet them, not for the bread (which the maid-servant bought) but to choose the **bread bangles**, or sometimes the sweet specially-made loaves. The baker always came twice a day — once early in the morning and again when he returned after emptying his basket. Baking was a **profitable profession**; the baker and his family never starved, and they always looked **fat and jolly** — even today, anyone with a jackfruit-like physique is compared to a baker. Bread is essential: **bol** (sweet bread) for marriage gifts, **bolinhas** and coconut cookies for Christmas, sandwiches for a daughter's engagement, and **pao** for the feast. The baker wore a peculiar dress, the **kabai**, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees; in the writer's childhood the bakers wore a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length ones. Monthly accounts were recorded on the wall in pencil, and the furnaces still exist.

**2. Coorg (Lokesh Abrol).** Coorg, or **Kodagu**, is the smallest district of Karnataka, midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore — a piece of heaven that must have drifted from the kingdom of god. It is a rolling hillside with a permanent fragrance of coffee, coffee estates and spice plantations, colonial bungalows under treetops, and forests. The season of joy is from **September to March**. The people of Coorg are a **proud race of martial men, beautiful women and wild creatures**; a popular theory traces their descent to **Alexander's army**, which moved south along the coast and settled there, marrying among the locals. Another theory claims **Arab origin**, since the **Kuppia**, the long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by the Kodavus, resembles the **kuffia** worn by the Arabs and the Kurds. Coorgis are the **most hospitable people in India**, and are the only people in India permitted to carry firearms without a licence. The **Kaveri river** originates from the hills and forests of Coorg; **Mahaseer**, a large freshwater fish, is found there, and kingfishers, squirrels, langurs and wild elephants can be seen. The climb to the **Brahmagiri hills** gives a view of the whole misty landscape of Coorg, and a walk to the sixty-acre **Buddhist monastery** at **Bylakuppe** is a surprise.

**3. Tea from Assam (Arup Kumar Datta).** Rajvir, a boy from Assam, travels to Delhi with Pranjol, whose father manages the **Dhekiajuli Tea Estate**. On the way they stop at a tea stall, where Rajvir hears that **eighty crore cups of tea are drunk every day throughout the world**. Pranjol's father meets them at Mariani junction and drives them through the **Dhekiajuli** estate, where acres of neatly pruned bushes stretch to the horizon with shade trees. Pranjol's mother welcomes them with tea and snacks. In the garden, the workers with bamboo baskets on their backs pluck the newly sprouted leaves. Pranjol's mother says that the Chinese legend says tea was first drunk in China around **2700 BC**, when some leaves from a burning twig fell into boiling water and gave a delicious drink; **Marco Polo** and **Bodhidharma** are also linked to tea legends. The second-sprouting period, from **May to July**, yields the finest tea. Tea was first brought to India from China by the British, and India now produces some of the finest tea in the world.
tricks: - **Pader, kabai, bol, bolinhas, pao** — five Goan words that anchor the Goa extract.
- **Coorg = coffee fragrance + martial men + firearms without licence + Kuppia coat.** Four markers, one paragraph.
- **Eighty crore cups a day** is the number asked most often in the Assam extract.
mistakes: - Saying Coorg is in Kerala. It is **Kodavu, in Karnataka**, the smallest district, between Mysore and Mangalore.
- Confusing **bol** (sweet bread for marriage gifts) with **bolinhas** (coconut cookies for Christmas).
- Giving the tea date as 2700 AD. The Chinese legend places it around **2700 BC**.

qa.a: Because he was woven into the daily life of the village. His arrival, announced by the jangling of his bamboo staff, was a fixed event twice a day, and children ran to meet him to choose their bread bangles. He was present at every celebration — bol for marriages, bolinhas and coconut cookies for Christmas, sandwiches for engagements — so his presence marked the family's important occasions.

One theory says they are descended from a part of Alexander's army that settled there and married among the locals; another says they are of Arab origin, because the Kuppia, the long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by the Kodavus, resembles the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds.

qa.q: Describe the Coorg landscape and its attractions.
a: Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka, lying midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore. It is a rolling hillside with a permanent fragrance of fresh coffee, coffee estates and spice plantations, colonial bungalows tucked under treetops, and dense forests.
**The best season** is from September to March, when the weather is perfect, the air breathes of invigorating coffee, and the rain showers keep the hills fresh.

**Attractions:** the climb to the Brahmagiri hills gives a panoramic view of the entire misty landscape of Coorg; a walk into the sixty-acre Buddhist monastery at Bylakutte, hidden among the coffee plantations, is a surprise; and there are rappelling, river rafting, canoeing and rock climbing for the adventurous.

An Indian legend says that Bodhidharma, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, cut off his eyelids because he felt sleepy during meditation, and ten tea plants grew out of the eyelids; the leaves of these plants, when put in hot water and drunk, banished sleep. Tea came to Europe only in the sixteenth century, and was drunk more as medicine than as a beverage.

title: Mijbil the Otter
short: Gavin Maxwell, an otter named Mijbil, and a journey to London.
lede: A true account of keeping an otter as a pet. The details — the water, the suitcase, the plane — are what is asked.

concepts: **1. Summary.** In **1956** the author, **Gavin Maxwell**, travelled to **Basra in Iraq** to the Consulate-General to collect and answer his mail from Europe. His pet otter had died, and his friend suggested he get an **otter from the Tigris marshes**. Two Arabs brought him a small otter in a sack — a creature he had never seen before, resembling most of all a small, medievally-conceived dragon. He named it **Mijbil**, and scientists later classified it as a previously unrecognised species, *Lutrogale perspicillata maxwelli*, or **Maxwell's otter**. Mijbil spent most of his time playing in the bathroom water, plunging and rolling in it, and shuffling on the tiled floor. When they went to **London**, Mijbil escaped from the box on the aeroplane, ran along the aircraft, and tore the lining to shreds, so Maxwell had to catch him — Mijbil came and sat on his knee and nuzzled his face. In London, Mijbil invented games with **marbles, ping-pong balls and rubber fruit**, and would play with them for hours. He learned to walk on a lead and developed compulsive habits, such as jumping over a low wall and running along the boundary wall of a school, where the children made noise. Londoners, who had never seen an otter, guessed that it was **'a baby seal', 'a squirrel', 'a walrus', 'a hippo', 'a beaver', 'a bear cub', 'a leopard'** or even **'a brontosaurus'**. Maxwell reflects that Mijbil seemed to have certain characteristics: he was, like a child, both **restless and full of joy**, and he had a strong need for the company and affection of human beings.

qa.q: What things does Mijbil do which tell you that he is an intelligent, friendly and fun-loving animal who needs love?
qa.a: He invented games with marbles, ping-pong balls and rubber fruit, and could keep himself amused for hours. He learned to walk on a lead and to respond to his name. He escaped from his box on the aeroplane, but instead of running away he came back and sat on Maxwell's knee and nuzzled his face — showing affection rather than fear. He developed compulsive rituals of his own, like the wall-jumping routine he repeated every day on the way to school, which shows both intelligence and a need for company.

Maxwell dived across the legs of other passengers to catch him, but Mijbil disappeared. When he returned to his seat he found the air-hostess with the otter on her knee. She had caught him and held him.
Mijbil then came back to Maxwell, sat on his knee and began to nuzzle his face and his neck, so the journey ended with the otter calm again, though the box was in tatters.

title: Madam Rides the Bus
short: Valliammai's eight-year-old journey, and what she learns on the way back.
lede: A child's independence and her first meeting with death — in one bus ride.
lens: Extracts from the planning of the journey, or from the return trip when Valli sees the dead cow.
Know her age (**eight years and some months**), the fare (**thirty paise each way**), the journey time (**forty-five minutes**), and what she refused on the bus.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Valliammai**, called **Valli** for short, was an eight-year-old girl — eight years and some months — who lived in a village. Her favourite pastime was standing in the **front doorway of her house** and watching what was happening in the street outside, because there were no other children of her own age. The sight that filled her with **unbelievable desire** was the bus that travelled between her village and the nearest town. It was a new bus, painted a gleaming white, with silver overhead bars; when it started, it seemed to be coming towards them, then turned and went back to the town. Day after day she watched it, and she gathered details by listening to conversations: the town was **six miles** away, the fare was **thirty paise one way**, and the trip took **forty-five minutes**. She saved the money by resisting every temptation to buy peppermints, toys and balloons, and by staying away from the merry-go-round at the village fair.

**2. The journey.** Valli stood up on her seat so that she could see everything: the bus ran along the bank of a canal, past palm trees, grassland, distant mountains and a blue sky. She saw a **young cow** running in front of the bus; the driver sounded the horn again and again, and the cow turned and looked at them and then ran faster, which made Valli laugh until tears filled her eyes. At the town, the conductor offered her a cold drink, but she refused and asked only to be taken back on the same bus. He called her **'madam'** throughout, and she insisted on being treated as an adult.

**3. The return.** On the way back, Valli saw the **same young cow lying dead by the roadside**, with her legs spread out, eyes lifeless and a fixed stare, and blood all over. She was horrified and had no desire to laugh any more. She did not want to look out of the window and sat glued to her seat. She reached her village at about **1:45 p.m.**, and found her mother awake and talking to an aunt. When her aunt asked where she had been, Valli's mother said she had been sleeping and had gone nowhere; Valli smiled to herself, because she had been so many places — and all without anyone knowing.

**4. Themes.** **Growing up and independence** — a child who plans and executes a journey alone. **Curiosity** — learning by listening and observing. **The first encounter with death** — the dead cow changes her, and the loss of innocence is the point of the ending.
tricks: - **Thirty paise each way, six miles, forty-five minutes.** Those three numbers are the most common 1-mark items.
- The **cow appears twice** — alive on the way out, dead on the way back. That contrast is the whole point of the story.
- The conductor calls her **'madam'** — hence the title.
mistakes: - Saying Valli took the bus with her mother. She went **alone**; that is the point.
- Giving her age as eight years. It is **eight years and some months**, which she is proud of.
- Missing the ending: Valli does not tell anyone, and her mother still thinks she was asleep.

qa.q: Why was the bus journey such a fascination for Valli?
qa.a: Because she had never been to the town and had no companions of her own age, so the bus became her window on the world. Every day it passed her house twice, carrying new people each time, and she longed to travel on it. The sight of the gleaming white bus, with its silver overhead bars and the people inside, filled her with an unbelievable desire, and the thought of travelling to the town and back grew stronger and stronger until she saved enough money to do it.

qa.q: What did Valli see on her way that made her laugh until tears filled her eyes?
qa.a: She saw a young cow whose tail was high in the air, running very fast right in the middle of the road in front of the bus. The driver sounded his horn again and again, but the more he honked the more frightened the cow became and the faster it ran. Valli found it so funny that she laughed and laughed until tears filled her eyes. On the return journey the same cow lay dead by the roadside, which filled her with horror and took away her joy.

qa.q: How did Valli plan her bus journey? What does this tell you about her?
a: **Planning:** she listened carefully to the conversations of her neighbours and of people who regularly used the bus, and she asked a few discreet questions here and there. From this she learnt that the town was six miles from her village, that the fare was thirty paise one way, and that the trip took forty-five minutes.

**Saving:** she resisted every temptation to buy peppermints, toys and balloons, and finally she even overcame her urge to ride the merry-go-round at the village annual fair, so that she could save sixty paise in all.
**Timing:** she chose to travel on the one o'clock afternoon bus, when her mother took her daily nap, so that she could be back before her mother woke.

**What it shows:** Valli was observant, determined and capable of self-control far beyond her years. She was also proud of being grown up — she resented being treated as a child, and insisted that the conductor call her madam.

qa.q: Why did Valli refuse the cold drink offered by the conductor?
qa.a: Because she had only sixty paise with her and wanted to keep enough for the return journey. Even though she was thirsty, she refused the drink and asked only to be taken back on the same bus. It shows her discipline and her determination to complete the plan she had made.

title: The Sermon at Benares
short: The Buddha, Kisa Gotami and the lesson of impermanence.
lede: A story about grief. The mustard-seed test is the heart of the answer.
lens: Extracts from Kisa Gotami's search and from the Buddha's sermon; a 5-mark answer on the Buddha's teaching about death.
Know the mustard-seed condition, why Kisa Gotami failed, and the words about the world being afflicted with decay and death.
concepts: **1. The Buddha's early life.** Born a prince named **Siddhartha Gautama**, he was married young and had a son. At about the age of twenty-five, while out hunting, he came upon a **sick man, then an aged man, then a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms**. These four sights so moved him that he left the palace at once and went out in search of enlightenment. He wandered for seven years and finally sat under a **fig (Bo) tree**, where he was enlightened. He then began to teach, and the tree was renamed the **Bo tree**. His first sermon was given at **Sarnath, near Benares**, on the banks of the Ganges, and has been preserved and is the subject of this chapter.

**2. Kisa Gotami's story.** **Kisa Gotami** had an only son, who died. Carrying the dead child, she went from house to house asking for medicine to cure him, and people thought she had lost her senses. At last a man directed her to the Buddha. The Buddha asked her to bring a **handful of mustard seed**, and when she promised to do so, he added the condition: the mustard seed must be taken from a house **where no one has died** — where no son, husband, parent or servant has been lost. Kisa Gotami went from door to door, and in every house someone had died: a father, a daughter, a servant, a slave. By evening she was weary and hopeless, and she sat down and watched the **lights of the city flicker and go out**; the darkness fell and spread. She understood at last the **selfishness of her grief**: she had been thinking only of her own loss, while death is common to all. She took the body of her child to the forest, laid it down, and returned to the Buddha.

**3. The sermon.** The Buddha said: **'Not from weeping nor from grief will anyone obtain peace of mind; on the contrary, his pain will be the greater and his body will suffer. He will make himself sick and pale, and yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation.'** Those who seek peace of mind should **draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief**; he who has drawn out the arrow and composed himself will obtain peace. The world is **afflicted with death and decay**, therefore the wise do not grieve, having realised the truth of the world. As a **ripe fruit is always in danger of falling**, so mortals, once born, are always in danger of dying. As **vessels made by the potter end by being broken**, so is the life of mortals. The wise, understanding the world, do not grieve. Grieving will not bring peace; it will only increase suffering.

**4. Themes.** **The universality of death** — every family has lost someone. **The futility of excessive grief** — it harms the living and cannot save the dead. **Enlightenment through experience** — the Buddha does not lecture Kisa Gotami; he makes her discover the truth herself. **Detachment and peace of mind.**
tricks: - The Buddha's method is a **test, not a lecture**: the mustard-seed condition makes Kisa Gotami find the answer herself.
- **'Draw out the arrow of lamentation'** is the key image — quote it in any answer about the sermon.
- **Potter's vessels break; ripe fruit falls.** Two similes that carry a full mark each.
mistakes: - Saying the Buddha refused to help Kisa Gotami. He gave her a **condition**, not a refusal.
- Forgetting that the mustard seed had to come from a house **where no one had died** — the condition is the whole point.
- Writing that the sermon was delivered at Bodh Gaya. It was at **Sarnath, near Benares**.

qa.q: Why did Kisa Gotami go from house to house, and what did she discover?
qa.a: Her only son had died, and she went from house to house asking for medicine to cure him. The Buddha told her to bring a handful of mustard seed, but on the condition that it be taken from a house where no one had died. In every house she entered, someone had died — a father, a daughter, a servant — so she could not find a single such house. She discovered that death is common to all, and that her grief had made her blind to the suffering of others.

qa.q: What did the Buddha say about grieving?
qa.a: He said that no one obtains peace of mind from weeping or from grief; on the contrary, the pain will be the greater and the body will suffer, and the person will make himself sick and pale, yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation. Those who seek peace of mind should draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief, and having drawn it out, they will obtain peace.

qa.q: How did the Buddha make Kisa Gotami understand the nature of death without preaching to her?
a: He did not tell her the truth directly. He asked her to bring him a handful of mustard seed — a simple request that gave her hope.
He then added one condition: the mustard seed must be taken from a house where no one had died, where no son, husband, parent or servant had been lost.

Kisa Gotami went from door to door with confidence, but in the first house she was told the father had died; in the next, a daughter; then a servant, then a slave. There was no house untouched by death.

By evening she was tired and hopeless. She sat and watched the lights of the city being lit and then going out until darkness covered everything, and she realised the selfishness of her grief — she had been absorbed in her own loss while death is common to all.

So the Buddha's method was to let her **experience** the truth rather than hear it, which is why it changed her completely. She took her child's body to the forest and returned to him ready to listen.

qa.q: Explain the meaning of 'the world is afflicted with death and decay, therefore the wise do not grieve'.
qa.a: It means that death and change are built into the world, so no amount of sorrow can prevent them. The wise understand this truth and accept it, so they do not grieve; they realise that lamentation cannot bring back the dead and only harms the living. Accepting the nature of the world is what brings peace of mind.

title: The Proposal
short: Chekhov's one-act farce about oxen meadows and hunting dogs.
lede: A play, not a story. Learn who says what, and never lose sight of the fact that the marriage proposal is never actually discussed.
lens: Extracts with a question on character or on the comedy; the two quarrels are the set 5-mark answer.
Know the three characters, the two disputes (**the Oxen Meadows**, then **Squeezer and Guess**), and the ages (**Lomov is 35, Natalya is 25**).
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Stepan Stepanovich Chubukov**, a wealthy landowner, is sitting in his drawing room in his house clothes. **Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov**, his neighbour, arrives dressed in evening clothes with gloves. Chubukov assumes he has come to borrow money, and complains that Lomov always comes to him for a loan. Lomov, nervous and stammering, asks permission to speak. Chubukov embraces him, thinking he has come to borrow money. Lomov then says that he has come to trouble him with a request — and Chubukov again thinks of money. Finally Lomov says that he has come to ask for the hand of **Natalya Stepanovna**, Chubukov's daughter. Chubukov is overjoyed, embraces and kisses him, and calls Natalya in. Before he can propose, Lomov and Natalya fall into a quarrel about the **Oxen Meadows**: Natalya claims the meadows belong to her, and Lomov insists they are his, saying his aunt's grandmother gave the free use of the meadows in perpetuity to the peasants of Chubukov's grandfather in return for making bricks. The argument grows, Chubukov joins in and insults Lomov, and Lomov leaves in a rage. Chubukov then reveals that Lomov had actually come to propose, and Natalya, realising this, begs her father to bring him back. Lomov returns, half-fainting, and Chubukov hurries the two into marriage. But before the proposal is settled, a second quarrel breaks out about hunting dogs — whether **Squeezer** (Lomov's dog) or **Guess** (Chubukov's) is the better dog — and the two men abuse each other again. Lomov collapses, and Chubukov blesses the couple: **'She's willing! Well, I'm sure enough!'** The play ends with the proposal achieved and the argument still going on.

**2. Characters.** **Lomov** — 35, a hypochondriac who suffers from palpitations, a twitching eyebrow and sleeplessness; timid, easily flustered and argumentative. **Chubukov** — loud, short-tempered and money-minded, but ready to push his daughter into a marriage. **Natalya Stepanovna** — 25, spoiled, quarrelsome and more interested in winning an argument than in marriage.

**3. The comedy.** The humour comes from the **contrast between the occasion and the behaviour**: a marriage proposal becomes a shouting match about a piece of land and then about a dog. Nobody ever speaks about love. Chekhov is satirising the **landowning class**, for whom property and possessions matter more than human feeling.
**4. Themes.** The **absurdity of the marriage market**; **greed and property**; **petty pride**; and the fact that people in a hurry to marry are not necessarily in love.
tricks: - **Two quarrels, one proposal that is never discussed.** That is the whole play in one line.
- **Lomov's ailments:** palpitations, twitching eyebrow, sleeplessness, numbness in the leg — a hypochondriac.
- The **Oxen Meadows** argument is about free use in perpetuity granted by an aunt's grandmother — the absurd chain of ownership is part of the joke.
mistakes: - Calling *The Proposal* a story by G. L. Fuentes. It is a **one-act play by Anton Chekhov**.
- Reversing the order of the quarrels: **Oxen Meadows first, then the dogs**.
- Saying Chubukov refuses the match. He is **delighted** and pushes it through, blessing the pair at the end.

qa.q: Why does Chubukov think Lomov has come to him?
qa.a: Because Lomov had come to him the previous year to borrow money, and Chubukov expects the same again. He even complains that Lomov is always coming to him for a loan, and when he hears that Lomov has a request, he assumes it is for money. Only when Lomov asks for Natalya's hand does Chubukov understand.

qa.q: What is the Oxen Meadows quarrel about?
qa.a: It is about who owns the Oxen Meadows, which lie between Lomov's Burnt Marsh and Chubukov's birchwood. Natalya insists the meadows are hers; Lomov says they are his, arguing that his aunt's grandmother gave the peasants of Chubukov's grandfather the free use of the meadows in perpetuity in return for their making bricks for her. The peasants had used them for forty years and regarded them as their own, but neither side will give way, and the argument turns into an exchange of insults.

qa.q: How does Chekhov use the two quarrels to create comedy and to criticise the characters?
a: **The first quarrel, about the Oxen Meadows,** begins before Lomov has even made his proposal. Natalya claims the meadows are hers, Lomov insists they are his, and both become abusive, calling each other a land grabber and an intriguess. Chubukov joins in, calls Lomov an old rat and a Jesuit, and orders him out of the house. The absurdity is that a marriage proposal has become a land dispute, and that Chubukov does not know what the proposal was until after the quarrel.

**The second quarrel, about the dogs,** follows immediately. Lomov praises his dog Squeezer; Chubukov insists his own Guess is better, and they argue over whether Squeezer's muzzle is short, whether Guess is purebred, and whether Squeezer's legs are crooked. The two men become hysterical and Lomov collapses.

**The criticism:** Chekhov shows that for these landowners, property and possessions matter far more than human relationships. Neither Lomov nor Natalya says a word about love or about each other's feelings, and the marriage is arranged in the middle of an argument. The comedy exposes a class that treats marriage as a transaction.

qa.q: Describe Lomov's character.
qa.a: Lomov is a thirty-five-year-old landowner who is timid, nervous and easily flustered. He is a hypochondriac: he complains of palpitations, a twitching right eyebrow, sleeplessness and numbness in his leg. He is also stubborn and quick to quarrel, which is why a marriage proposal turns into two arguments. Yet he is sincere in his wish to settle down, and he finally gets what he came for.

qa.q: How does the play end? Comment on the ending.
qa.a: Lomov collapses after the argument about the dogs, and Chubukov, without waiting for anything to be settled, blesses the couple and cries that Natalya is willing, calling for champagne. Natalya does not object, and the proposal is agreed. The ending is comic because the marriage is decided in the middle of a quarrel that neither side has stopped fighting — nobody has spoken a word about love, and the audience is left to see how absurd the whole arrangement is.
